title: Cement dust: a negative production externality, the external cost and why the efficient amount is not zero
scenario: In an invented region, many perfectly competitive firms make cement. Dust from the plants dirties nearby homes and costs residents $3 for every ton of cement produced. No one outside the market gains from it, and the plants do not pay for the damage.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw a correctly labeled graph of the cement market showing demand, supply and marginal social cost. Show the socially efficient quantity, labeled QE.

rubric.point: A correctly labeled graph: Price and Quantity on the axes, D (= MPB = MSB), S (= MPC) and MSC above S
accept: P and Q on the axes
D, S or MPC, and MSC labeled, with MSC above S

rubric.point: QE shown where MSC crosses demand (MSB), at a smaller quantity than where S crosses demand

parts.sample: Price is on the vertical axis and Quantity on the horizontal axis. D = MPB = MSB slopes down; S = MPC slopes up; MSC lies above S by the $3 external cost per ton. The market quantity QM is where D meets S. The efficient quantity QE, where D meets MSC, is to the left of QM and is marked with a dashed line to the quantity axis.

slips.S: Supply shows only the plants' own costs; the efficient point uses MSC, which includes the dust.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Shade the area that shows the total external cost of the dust at the market quantity.

rubric.point: The area between MSC and S (= MPC) from zero to the market quantity, fully shaded
accept: the band between MSC and supply out to QM

parts.sample: The external cost is $3 for each ton produced, so the total is the band between MSC and S, from zero out to the market quantity QM, where demand meets S.

slips.dwl: That triangle is the deadweight loss. The external cost counts the $3 of damage on every ton produced, from zero to QM.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain why the socially efficient quantity of cement is not zero, even though every ton produces dust.

rubric.point: Up to QE, the marginal social benefit of each ton (shown by demand) is greater than its marginal social cost, including the $3 of dust damage, so producing those tons adds to total surplus
accept: MSB > MSC for the tons up to QE
the benefit of the first tons is greater than their private cost plus the $3 of damage

parts.sample: The efficient quantity is where MSB = MSC, not where the damage is zero. For every ton up to QE, buyers value the cement (MSB, shown by demand) more than it costs society to make, including the $3 of dust damage, so producing those tons makes society better off. Only tons beyond QE cost more than they are worth.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Suppose the dust damage were $5 a ton instead of $3. Identify what would happen to the deadweight loss of the market outcome, and explain.

rubric.point: The deadweight loss would increase, because MSC would lie further above supply, so the efficient quantity is smaller and the market overproduces more tons, each with a larger gap between MSC and MSB
accept: it increases: a bigger gap between MSC and S, so more overproduction

parts.sample: The deadweight loss would increase. With $5 of damage per ton, MSC lies further above S, so it crosses demand at a smaller efficient quantity, while the market quantity, where D meets S, does not change. The market now overproduces more tons, and on each of them MSC exceeds MSB by more, so the triangle grows.
